summary: Describes a simple Remote Write Protocol (RWP). It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A simple way to send a message so it shows up on someone else's screen.

questions: what is the remote write protocol
how do you send a message with rwp
subtitle: A lightweight network protocol for delivering short interactive messages between users.

tldr.problem: Users need a simpler alternative to email and talk for exchanging quick messages across a network.
tldr.mechanism: RWP is a command-response protocol where a client connects to a server and issues commands to send a message: FROM (sender), TO (recipient), DATA (message content), and SEND.
tldr.outcome: The server returns status codes indicating success or failure of each operation, and delivers the message to the recipient's terminal if they are logged in.

today: RFC 1756 is an Experimental protocol and has not been obsoleted. It remains a historical specification; RWP was not widely adopted, and modern systems use instant messaging, email, or chat protocols instead.

sections.title: Background and Overview
sections.content:
RFC 1756 defines the Remote Write Protocol (RWP), a simple protocol for relaying short messages through a network to other users. It fills a gap between the heaviness of electronic mail and synchronous tools like the UNIX talk program, offering something similar to the UNIX write command but working across networks.

The protocol is designed to be straightforward, resembling SMTP but adapted for the interactive nature of message delivery. A client program connects to an RWP server running on the target machine and exchanges commands and responses to deliver a message to a recipient. RWP supports both TCP (which returns status after each action) and UDP (which broadcasts messages without responses).
sections.plainLanguage: RWP is a way to send a short message to someone on another computer, like the write command you can use on one computer but across networks. The server tells you whether it worked.

sections.title: Protocol Commands and Message Flow
sections.content:
An RWP session follows a predictable sequence. When the client connects, the server announces it is ready with response code 100. The client then issues commands to identify the sender, recipient, and message body.

Status query commands help the client learn about the server: HELP lists available commands, HELO greets the server, PROT requests the protocol version, VRFY checks if a recipient exists and can receive messages, and VER requests the server program version.

Message handling commands are the core of the protocol. FROM specifies the sender's login, TO specifies the recipient (optionally with a particular terminal), FHST records the original host and forwarding path for relayed messages, DATA begins message input (terminated by a single dot on a line), and SEND submits the message for delivery. The FWDS command tracks how many times a message has been forwarded, with a server-specific limit to prevent infinite loops.

Session control commands manage the connection: RSET resets the session state, BYE terminates cleanly with response code 101, and QUIT is an impolite synonym for BYE. A QUOTE command allows server-specific extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: To send a message, you tell the server who you are (FROM), who to send it to (TO), then give the message (DATA), then say SEND. The server replies after each step to let you know if it worked.

sections.title: Response Codes and Error Handling
sections.content:
Every RWP server action produces a response: a three-digit numeric code and a short text explanation. The code determines what the client should do next.

Success codes in the 100s and 200s indicate successful operations: 100 (Ready), 103 (Message delivered), 104 (Message forwarded), 105-107 (FROM, TO, DATA ok), 108 (Recipient ok to send), and 200 (Enter message). Group 300 carries autoreply messages from the recipient, each line prefixed with 300 and a pipe character.

Error codes 668-699 report failures. Syntax errors produce 668. Delivery failures include 669 (Permission denied), 670 (User not logged in), 671 (No such user), and 672 (Empty message). Operational errors include missing required commands before SEND (673-675), exceeding forwarding limits (676), inability to forward (677), and unknown errors (698-699).

For character set safety, RWP uses MIME-like quoted-printable encoding: special characters are represented as an equals sign followed by two hex digits (e.g., =2E for a dot, =3D for an equals sign). This prevents dots in message bodies from terminating the message prematurely.
sections.plainLanguage: The server uses number codes to tell you what happened: numbers like 103 mean success, numbers like 670 mean the person isn't logged in. The codes follow patterns so you can predict what they mean.

sections.title: Deployment and Messaging Delivery
sections.content:
RWP is designed to run on TCP and UDP ports, with port 18 proposed as the standard in the /etc/services file. The protocol is transport-agnostic about how the message is actually presented to the recipient; the basic approach is a write to the user's terminal (matching the UNIX write behavior), but servers can implement configurable delivery methods.

For systems supporting multiple connected networks, an End System may forward a message by adding it to a forwarding path (FHST command) and incrementing a hop counter (FWDS command). This allows RWP messages to traverse multiple networks, though servers enforce a maximum forwarding count to prevent loops. When forwarding is not possible or the limit is exceeded, the server returns an appropriate error and the client may choose to attempt direct delivery despite the restriction.

The reference implementation RWrite-1.0 includes support for user configuration files allowing recipients to permit or deny messages from specific users, hosts, or network domains. Message agents (per-user processes) are under development to provide more sophisticated filtering and delivery options.
sections.plainLanguage: RWP runs on a specific port on the remote computer. The message usually appears on the person's screen. If they're not there, the server can forward the message to another server, or tell you the delivery failed.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
RWP version 1.0 has significant security limitations inherited from its design as a simple protocol. The protocol offers no means to verify the identity of connecting users, analogous to SMTP's weakness. While it is possible to identify the sender using the ident service, not all hosts support it. This vulnerability allows any client to claim to be any user.

The server may inadvertently reveal valid user IDs through responses to TO and VRFY commands: responding with 671 (no such user) discloses whether an account exists. Servers can mitigate this by always returning 670 (user not logged in) instead, obscuring the difference between non-existent and offline users.

A hostile sender could flood a user's terminal with unwanted messages. Servers can limit this exposure by delivering messages through a per-user agent process rather than directly to the terminal; such agents can decide whether to accept messages and how to display them.

Cryptographic user verification and message encryption are acknowledged as missing features. RFC 1756 notes that these are under development for RWP version 2.0, planned for 1995. Until then, RWP is suitable only for environments where users trust the network and each other.
sections.plainLanguage: The big problem is that RWP doesn't check who you really are before sending a message. Anyone could pretend to be someone else. Also, someone could send you a lot of unwanted messages and mess up your screen. A better version with passwords and encryption was planned but not in version 1.0.
